==Problem 19==
The first three terms of a geometric sequence are the integers <imath>a,\,720,</imath> and <imath>b,</imath> where <imath>a<720<b.</imath> What is the sum of the digits of the least possible value of <imath>b?</imath>

<imath>\textbf{(A) } 9 \qquad \textbf{(B) } 12 \qquad \textbf{(C) } 16 \qquad \textbf{(D) } 18 \qquad \textbf{(E) } 21</imath>

==Solution 1==
For a geometric sequence, we have <imath>ab=720^2=2^8 3^4 5^2</imath>, and we can test values for <imath>b</imath>. We find that <imath>b=768</imath> and <imath>a=675</imath> works, and we can test multiples of <imath>5</imath> in between the two values. Finding that none of the multiples of 5 divide <imath>720^2</imath> besides <imath>720</imath> itself, we know that the answer is <imath>7+6+8=\boxed{\textbf{(E) } 21}</imath>.

(Note: To find the value of <imath>b</imath> without bashing, we can observe that <imath>2^8=256</imath>, and that multiplying it by <imath>3</imath> gives us <imath>768</imath>, which is really close to <imath>720</imath>. ~ YTH)

Note: The reason why <imath>ab=720^2</imath> is because <imath>b/720 = 720/a</imath>. Rearranging this gives <imath>ab = 720^2</imath>

~eevee9406

Note: Another reason that <imath>ab=720^2</imath> is because the <imath>\sqrt{ab}=720</imath> (as the middle term in a geometric series is always the geometric mean [the geometric mean is the square root of the product of the first and last terms of the series]) and squaring on both sides results in <imath>ab=720^2</imath>.

~ThatPrimePunnyGuy

==Solution 2==
<imath>720 = 2^4 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 5</imath>. We want to find factors <imath>x</imath> and <imath>y</imath> where <imath>y>x</imath> such that <imath>\frac{y}{x}</imath>, the ratio, is minimized. To do this, <imath>x</imath> should be as large as possible, and <imath>y</imath> should be just slightly larger than <imath>x</imath>. Additionally, to ensure <imath>a</imath> and <imath>b</imath> are both integers, <imath>x</imath> and <imath>y</imath> should both be a factor of <imath>720</imath>.

After experimenting, we see this is achieved when <imath>y=16</imath> and <imath>x=15</imath>, which means our value of <imath>b</imath> is <imath>720 \cdot \frac{16}{15} = 768</imath>. Therefore, the sum is <imath>7+6+8=\boxed{\textbf{(E) } 21}</imath>.

~i_am_suk_at_math_2

== Solution 3 (Similar to previous solutions) ==

To minimize the value of <imath>b</imath>, where it has to be an integer, and it has to be greater than 720, we can express the common ratio as <imath>\dfrac{n+1}{n}</imath>, where the value has to be greater than <imath>1</imath>, and <imath>n</imath>, and <imath>n+1</imath> have to be factors of 720. Since the bigger the denominator gets, the smaller the value of the fraction, we essentially have to find the biggest value for <imath>n</imath>, where itself and <imath>n+1</imath> are factors of <imath>720</imath>. From here, we can check whether <imath>n(n+1) = 720</imath> yields an integer root, which it doesn't. So, then we check the next biggest factor of <imath>720</imath>, which is <imath>360</imath>. <imath>n(n+1) = 360</imath>, this doesn't have an integer root either. So, then we check the next biggest factor which is <imath>240</imath>, <imath>n(n+1) = 240</imath>, which we get <imath>15</imath> as a root. This means the common ration is <imath>\dfrac{16}{15}</imath>. We then multiply <imath>\dfrac{16}{15}</imath> times <imath>720</imath> and add up the digits getting <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(E) } 21}</imath>.

~yuvag

== Solution 4 ==

Let the common ratio of the geometric sequence be <imath>\frac{x}{y}</imath>, with <imath>x>y</imath>. This means that <imath>720(\frac{x}{y})</imath> and <imath>720(\frac{y}{x})</imath> must both be integers, therefore <imath>x</imath> and <imath>y</imath> are both factors of <imath>720</imath>. We would achieve the smallest ratio <imath>\frac{x}{y}</imath> if <imath>x</imath> and <imath>y</imath> are consecutive, so by listing out the factors of <imath>720</imath>, we find that <imath>1</imath>, <imath>2</imath>, <imath>3</imath>, <imath>4</imath>, <imath>5</imath>, <imath>6</imath>, <imath>8</imath>, <imath>9</imath>, <imath>10</imath>, <imath>15</imath>, <imath>16</imath> are the only consecutive factors (any factors larger than these would result in the ratio simplifying, making it larger than just using consecutive integers). <imath>15</imath> and <imath>16</imath> are the largest, so we find the common ratio to be <imath>\frac{16}{15}</imath>, making <imath>b=720(\frac{16}{15})</imath> giving us <imath>768</imath>. The sum of its digits is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(E) } 21}</imath>.

~lisztepos

==Solution 5 (similar to other solutions) ==
We look for the smallest possible increasing ratio in the geometric sequence for <imath>a</imath>, <imath>720</imath>, and <imath>b</imath>.
First, we find the prime factorization of <imath>720</imath>, which is really easy <imath>720=2^4\cdot3^2\cdot5</imath>. Then, we look for the closest possible fraction-ratio out of the primes, and after a quick look, it's easy to see it is <imath>16</imath> and <imath>15</imath>. Now that we found our ratio, we multiply <imath>720</imath> by <imath>\frac{16}{15}</imath> to get <imath>768</imath>, so the sum of the digits of the least possible value of <imath>b</imath> is <imath>21</imath>.

~hashbrown2009
